title: This week AI helped people speak, sign and get around. (Saturday 21 Nov good news, off-sat-goodnews, approved by Krish Wed 18 Nov 11:13)
experiment: The Saturday rule's source and date ride in the designed mono kicker on every story card (no footer strip), and the cover is a photo-grade street scene with the house robot as an over-keen tour guide leading a delighted crowd.

five_whys.q: Why is this week good news?
five_whys.a: Five AI tools went on sale, into testing or into daily use that help people speak, sign, read and get around on their own.

five_whys.q: Why did five arrive in one week?
five_whys.a: AI that hears, speaks, reads and sees is now ready-made, so tiny teams build on it: two Montreal founders on ElevenLabs' voice AI, one 17-year-old in India.

five_whys.q: Why does that matter more than another lab demo?
five_whys.a: Real people use them: a woman with ALS talks in her own voice every day, Glide is reaching its first customers, and a deaf teacher scored Thatsign 9 out of 10.

five_whys.q: Why is it bigger than five stories?
five_whys.a: The World Health Organization says over 2.5 billion people need help such as glasses, hearing aids or wheelchairs, and in many countries most go without.

five_whys.q: Why should an everyday business person care?
five_whys.a: The same gap sits in their own business: a PDF or web page a screen reader cannot read shuts a customer out, and checking takes five minutes on a phone.

explains.ALS: a disease that slowly takes away speech and movement (card 2 says she lost her speech to it)
explains.screen reader: the free setting on every phone that reads the screen aloud (card 9 names VoiceOver and TalkBack)

cards.headline: This week AI helped people speak, sign and get around.
cards.line: A woman with ALS talks in her own voice again, and four more stories like hers.
cards.picture: Photo-grade generated street scene: the hand-sewn felt house robot as an over-keen tour guide, mint flag held high and a tiny megaphone, leading a delighted crowd across a city zebra crossing at golden hour; in the crowd a blind man with a white cane, a mum signing to her small daughter, an older woman laughing as she speaks. The house robot's two reference photos passed to the model.

cards.headline: An AI app gives a Montreal woman who lost her speech to ALS her own voice back.
cards.line: ALS is a disease that takes away speech; Vocality built her voice from recordings of her talking.
cards.picture: The real Canadian Press photo (Christinne Muschi, 10 Nov): Anne-Marie Poirier with her iPad, the two co-founders beside her

story_source.label: The Canadian Press via MTL Blog, 11 Nov 2026

cards.headline: A new app in testing lets hearing parents and deaf children talk, turning speech into signs and signs into words.
cards.line: Thatsign, still in testing, is for the hearing parents of more than 9 in 10 deaf children.
cards.picture: The real Techpoint Africa photo (supplied): Confidence Ugolo working on the Thatsign dashboard

cards.headline: Glide, an AI guide that steers blind people around obstacles, is reaching its first customers.
cards.line: Ask it out loud, and it tells you what is around you.
cards.picture: Glidance's own photo of a person walking with Glide, its handle in hand

cards.headline: Google's new AI glasses describe the world to blind wearers and read small print aloud.
cards.line: The feature is called Guided Vision, and the glasses go on sale on 10 December.
cards.picture: Google's own lifestyle photo of a person wearing the new glasses

cards.headline: A 17-year-old built an AI tool that lets blind people read bank statements by themselves.
cards.line: Yash Bhatnagar's Visionably, built in India, works on about 95% of the PDFs it is tested on.
cards.picture: A real photo of Yash Bhatnagar from The Better India's article (never its AI-generated lead image); else a real Visionably screen

cards.headline: Small teams build helpers for disabled people, because they can buy AI that hears, speaks and sees.
cards.line: Two founders built Vocality on ElevenLabs' voice AI, and one teenager built Visionably.
cards.picture: Photo-grade scene: a cluttered kitchen-table workshop at night, one laptop, a phone, a pair of smart glasses, a small wheeled walking guide and a mug under a desk lamp: a tiny team, big help

cards.headline: The World Health Organization says over 2.5 billion people need help such as glasses, hearing aids or wheelchairs.
cards.line: In many countries most go without, which is why cheap AI helpers like these matter.
cards.picture: Photo-grade aerial of a vast city crowd at dusk, a scattering of people with white canes, hearing aids and wheelchairs lit warm among them
cards.source: World Health Organization, fact sheet 'Assistive technology' (read 18 Nov 2026): 'Globally, more than 2.5 billion people need one or more assistive products'; 3.5 billion by 2050; 'In many countries, most people who need assistive technology do not have access to it.' https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/assistive-technology

cards.headline: Try your phone's free screen reader on your business's PDFs to hear what blind customers hear.
cards.line: VoiceOver on iPhone and TalkBack on Android are built in; whatever they skip, a blind customer misses.
cards.picture: Photo-grade close-up: a hand holding a phone over a business invoice PDF, the screen reader's black focus box around one line, earbuds beside it

cards.picture: His fixed good-news close: the five story photos in mint rings on a soft green glow, in story order
cards.cta: If this inspires you to MAKE THE WORLD BETTER by combining your ideas + AI, follow for more

read_back.reader: fresh reader K (Sonnet, headlines only, once)

answers.what: Good news about AI helping disabled people: this week's examples cover speech, sign language and navigation or reading for blind people.
answers.happened: Several AI tools were announced or reached users: an app gave a Montreal woman with ALS her own voice back, a sign-language app is in testing for hearing parents and deaf children, and Glide, an AI guide for blind people, is reaching its first customers. Google AI glasses describe the world and read small print aloud, and a 17-year-old built a tool to read bank statements for blind people.
answers.why: Because AI that can hear, speak and see is now good enough to buy, so small teams can build helpers for disabled people.
answers.so_what: Over 2.5 billion people need assistive help, such as glasses, hearing aids or wheelchairs, so tools like these could matter to a lot of people. It may also matter if you run a business with blind customers.
answers.do: Try your phone's free screen reader on your own PDFs to hear what blind customers hear. If inspired, build something that combines your ideas with AI, and follow for more.

answers.what: New AI tools are helping disabled people talk, sign and get around, and the post shows several examples.
answers.happened: This week AI apps and devices were reported that help people who are blind, deaf or who lost their speech, including a voice app for an ALS patient, a speech-to-sign app in testing, a guide that steers blind people around obstacles, Google glasses that describe the world, and a 17-year-old's bank statement reader.
answers.why: Small teams are building these helpers because AI that can hear, speak and see is now good enough to sell.
answers.so_what: A lot of people need this kind of help, over 2.5 billion by the World Health Organization's count, and it is getting cheaper and easier to make, so more of them may get it.
answers.do: Try your phone's free screen reader on a PDF to hear what a blind person hears, then think about how you could mix your own ideas with AI to help someone.
